blocks.text: The energy needed to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state (always positive, endothermic). Bond making is the same size but negative.
The average bond enthalpy of 1 mole of a particular covalent bond over a range of compounds, e.g. C–H = ¼ of ΔH<sub>at</sub>(CH<sub>4</sub>).
The enthalpy change when 1 mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states. ΔH<sub>f</sub> of an element in its standard state = 0.
The enthalpy change when 1 mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element in its standard state (e.g. Na(s) → Na(g)). Always endothermic.
The energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in 1 mole of gaseous atoms: M(g) → M<sup>+</sup>(g) + e<sup>-</sup>. Endothermic.
The enthalpy change when 1 mole of gaseous atoms gains one electron each: X(g) + e<sup>-</sup> → X<sup>-</sup>(g). Usually exothermic (2nd E.A. of oxygen is endothermic).
The enthalpy change when 1 mole of a crystal is formed from its constituent ions in the gaseous phase (exothermic).
Application of Hess's law linking the standard enthalpy changes in the formation of an ionic compound, used to find the lattice enthalpy.
The enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken, provided initial and final conditions are the same.
How much more stable benzene is than the Kekulé structure: 176 kJ/mol (calculated −384 vs experimental −208).
A mixture with no volume change and no enthalpy change on mixing; its boiling point is the weighted average of the components'.
The component with the higher vapour pressure and lower boiling point (higher tendency to escape into the vapour).
Separation of liquids by repeated vaporisation and condensation, giving the more volatile component first.

A mixture with a constant boiling point and the same composition in liquid and vapour; cannot be separated by fractional distillation. Minimum (positive deviation) or maximum (negative deviation) boiling.
The constant ratio of a solute's concentration in two immiscible solvents at equilibrium, e.g. [X]<sub>CCl<sub>4</sub></sub> / [X]<sub>H<sub>2</sub>O</sub>.
A chemically distinct substance in the system (water is a one-component system; water + ethanol is two-component).
The factors that can change independently in a system: temperature and pressure for a one-component system.
A graph summarising the temperature and pressure conditions under which each phase of a substance is stable.
The temperature and pressure at which solid, liquid and vapour are all in equilibrium (water: 273.16 K, ~0.006 atm).
The end of the vapour pressure curve: above the critical temperature the vapour cannot be condensed whatever the pressure (water: 647 K, 218 atm).
A reaction that can go forward and backward (⇌).
The state in which the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction (dynamic, closed system, constant temperature, no observable change).

blocks.title: Formula and signs
lines: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed). Breaking is endothermic (+); making is exothermic (−). Bond enthalpies are always positive numbers.

blocks.text: Diatomic: bond enthalpy X–X = 2 × ΔH<sub>at</sub>(X) (Cl–Cl = 2 × 122 = 244).
Mean C–H in methane = ¼ ΔH<sub>at</sub>(CH<sub>4</sub>) = ¼ × 1662 = +415.5 kJ/mol.
Use the values GIVEN in the question (your notes use C–Cl = 326; the table shows 339).

blocks.title: Calculate ΔH from bond enthalpies
blocks.task: Use the bond enthalpies in the notes to estimate ΔH for H<sub>2</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2HCl.
steps: Bonds broken: one H–H bond and one Cl–Cl bond. Add 436 + 244 = 680 kJ/mol.
Bonds formed: two H–Cl bonds. Add 2 × 431 = 862 kJ/mol.
Apply ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed: 680 − 862.

blocks.task: Using the bond-enthalpy values in the notes, calculate the energy difference between the predicted Kekulé hydrogenation (−384 kJ/mol) and experimental hydrogenation (−208 kJ/mol).

sections.title: Enthalpy of formation: reactions and stability

blocks.title: Formulae
lines: ΔH<sub>R</sub> = ΣnΔH<sub>f</sub>(products) − ΣnΔH<sub>f</sub>(reactants). Elements in standard state: ΔH<sub>f</sub> = 0.
Hess: ΔH<sub>f</sub>(CH<sub>4</sub>) = ΔH<sub>c</sub>(C) + 2ΔH<sub>c</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>) − ΔH<sub>c</sub>(CH<sub>4</sub>) = −393 + 2(−286) + 890 = −75 kJ/mol.

rows: ½N<sub>2</sub> + 3/2 H<sub>2</sub>O(g) → NH<sub>3</sub> + ¾O<sub>2</sub>; NH<sub>3</sub> −46.2, H<sub>2</sub>O(g) −242

items: Stability: very negative ΔH<sub>f</sub> (CO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O, Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) = stable relative to elements; large positive ΔH<sub>f</sub> = unstable, decomposes easily.
H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>: ΔH<sub>f</sub> = −210 (stable vs H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub>) but decomposes to H<sub>2</sub>O + ½O<sub>2</sub> (exothermic). Always say 'stable with respect to what'.
Feasibility: more negative ΔH = more likely to occur; endothermic can still occur (spontaneity also depends on entropy).

Substitute the values: −393 + 2(−286) − (−890).

blocks.text: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of a crystal is formed from its constituent ions in the gaseous phase. Cannot be measured directly: found from the Born-Haber cycle (Hess's law).

−411 = 108 + 495 + 122 − 360 + ΔH lattice → ΔH lattice = −776 kJ/mol.

blocks.title: Calculate NaCl lattice enthalpy
blocks.task: Use the Born–Haber values in the notes to find the lattice enthalpy of NaCl.
steps: Write the cycle equation: ΔH<sub>f</sub> = ΔH<sub>at</sub>(Na) + 1st I.E.(Na) + ΔH<sub>at</sub>(Cl) + E.A.(Cl) + ΔH<sub>lattice</sub>.
Substitute: −411 = 108 + 495 + 122 − 360 + ΔH<sub>lattice</sub>.
Add the known terms: 108 + 495 + 122 − 360 = 365.
Rearrange to isolate the lattice enthalpy: −411 − 365.

blocks.title: Three properties of an ideal solution
lines: No volume change on mixing. No enthalpy change on mixing. Boiling point = weighted average of the components' boiling points.

items: More volatile component: higher vapour pressure, LOWER boiling point.
Vapour is richer in the more volatile component; repeated condensation and re-boiling (fractional distillation) gives it pure first; the other stays in the flask.
b.pt-composition diagram = inverted v.p.-composition diagram.

blocks.title: Calculate an ideal mixture’s boiling point
blocks.task: Find the boiling point of an ideal mixture containing 70% methylbenzene (111 °C) and 30% benzene (80 °C). Which component is more volatile?
steps: Use the weighted average: (0.70 × 111) + (0.30 × 80).
Calculate each contribution: 77.7 + 24.
Compare the pure boiling points: the lower boiling point means greater volatility.
blocks.answer: The ideal mixture’s boiling point is 101.7 °C. Benzene is more volatile and distils first.

blocks.text:
An azeotrope (say 'AY-zee-oh-trope') is a mixture of two liquids that boils like a single pure liquid.
• It boils at ONE fixed temperature (not a range).
• The vapour that comes off has the same mixture (same percentages) as the liquid in the flask.
• Because of this, you cannot separate the two liquids any further by fractional distillation.

blocks.term: Textbook definition (use this in an exam)
blocks.text: An azeotropic mixture is a mixture that has a constant boiling point and constant composition. When it is heated, the liquid and the vapour have the same composition, so it cannot be separated by fractional distillation.
Why can't we separate it? (3 steps)

items: Normal distillation works because the vapour has MORE of the liquid that boils easily. We collect that vapour, cool it, and boil it again: each round gives a purer liquid.
At the azeotrope the vapour has the SAME recipe as the liquid. Boiling changes nothing.
So no matter how many times you repeat the distillation, the recipe stays the same and the liquids stay mixed.

blocks.text: Think of it like this: a sieve that lets both liquids through at exactly the same rate cannot separate them.
Two types

rows: a LOWER temperature than either liquid alone
a HIGHER temperature than either liquid alone
The two liquids 'don't mix happily': their particles escape into vapour more easily, so the mixture boils sooner
The two liquids 'like each other': their particles hold on tighter, so it needs more heat to boil
ethanol + benzene; ethanol + water; ethanol + trichloromethane; propanone + carbon disulphide
water + nitric acid; trichloromethane + propanone; methanoic acid + water

blocks.text: What do I collect, and what is left in the flask?

rows: LEFT of the azeotrope on the graph (extra B)
Azeotrope comes out FIRST. Pure B is left in the flask.
Pure B comes out FIRST. Azeotrope is left in the flask.
Azeotrope comes out FIRST. Pure A is left in the flask.
Pure A comes out FIRST. Azeotrope is left in the flask.

lines: Minimum azeotrope = the easiest thing to boil, so it escapes first.
Maximum azeotrope = the hardest thing to boil, so it stays behind in the flask and the extra liquid comes out first.

blocks.text: Extra real-life fact (not in your notes): ethanol and water form a minimum azeotrope of about 96% ethanol, which is why simple distillation cannot give 100% pure ethanol.

blocks.question: What is an azeotrope in one sentence?
blocks.answer: A mixture of two liquids that boils at a constant temperature and gives a vapour with the same composition as the liquid.

blocks.question: Can fractional distillation separate an azeotrope?
blocks.answer: No, because liquid and vapour have the same composition.

blocks.question: Ethanol + water mixture is boiled. What type is it?
Max azeotrope: which part comes out first?
blocks.answer: The pure liquid that is in excess; the azeotrope stays in the flask.

blocks.title: Predict what distils from a maximum azeotrope mixture
blocks.task: A mixture lies to the left of a maximum-boiling azeotrope on the composition graph, so it contains extra B. What comes out first and what remains in the flask?
steps: Identify the type: this is a maximum-boiling azeotrope.
Locate the starting composition: it is left of the azeotrope and contains extra B.
Use the maximum-azeotrope distillation rule for a mixture left of the azeotrope.
blocks.answer: Pure B comes out first; the azeotrope is left in the flask.

blocks.title: K = [X]<sub>CCl<sub>4</sub></sub> / [X]<sub>water</sub> = 4; 20 g in water; equal volumes
lines: 1st: y/(20 − y) = 4 → y = 16 g (4 g left). 2nd on the 4 g: z/(4 − z) = 4 → 5z = 16 → z = 3.2 g. Total = 19.2 g (vs 16 g in one go).
Rule: several small extractions beat one big one.

blocks.text: Starting mass 20 g is inferred (top of the page is cut off in the photo).

blocks.title: Compare two small solvent extractions
blocks.task: K = [X]<sub>CCl<sub>4</sub></sub> / [X]<sub>water</sub> = 4. Extract 20 g of X in water twice using equal volumes of CCl<sub>4</sub>. How much X is removed in total?
steps: For the first extraction, let y be the mass transferred: y/(20 − y) = 4, so y = 16 g. There are 4 g left in water.
For the second extraction, let z be the mass transferred from the remaining 4 g: z/(4 − z) = 4.
Solve: z = 3.2 g. Add the portions removed: 16 + 3.2.
blocks.answer: 19.2 g is extracted in total; 0.8 g remains in water.

items: Reaction goes to completion when a reactant is used up (CaCO<sub>3</sub> + 2HCl → CaCl<sub>2</sub> + CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O).
Reversible reaction: can go forward and backward, shown by ⇌ (Ag<sup>+</sup> + Fe<sup>2+</sup> ⇌ Ag + Fe<sup>3+</sup>).
Equilibrium: forward rate = reverse rate.
Characteristics: closed system; at a particular temperature; no observable change; dynamic (both reactions still happening).

blocks.title: Describe a system at equilibrium
blocks.task: A reversible reaction is in a closed vessel at constant temperature. The measured concentrations stop changing, although both reactions continue. Explain whether it is at equilibrium.
steps: Check that the reaction is reversible, so forward and reverse reactions both occur.
At equilibrium, the forward rate equals the reverse rate; the reactions do not stop.
In a closed system at constant temperature, equal rates produce no observable change in concentrations.
blocks.answer: Yes. It is dynamic equilibrium: the forward and reverse rates are equal, with no observable change in the closed system at constant temperature.
